# --description--

`new Set()` accepts any **iterable**, not just arrays. A string is iterable character by character, so it gives you the distinct characters of a text:
```javascript
let letters = new Set("hello");
console.log([...letters]);
// prints [ 'h', 'e', 'l', 'o' ]
```

# --instructions--

Write a function `commonLetters(a, b)` that returns an array with the characters that appear in both strings, without duplicates and in the order they first appear in `a`

# --asserts--

`commonLetters("hello", "world")` must return `["l", "o"]`.

```javascript
tryCatch(JSON.stringify(commonLetters("hello", "world")) === '["l","o"]');
```

`commonLetters("abc", "xyz")` must return `[]`.

```javascript
tryCatch(JSON.stringify(commonLetters("abc", "xyz")) === '[]');
```

`commonLetters("banana", "nab")` must return `["b", "a", "n"]`.

```javascript
tryCatch(JSON.stringify(commonLetters("banana", "nab")) === '["b","a","n"]');
```

# --solutions--

```javascript
function commonLetters(a, b) {
  let lettersB = new Set(b);
  return [...new Set(a)].filter((ch) => lettersB.has(ch));
}
```
